content.title: Global Marketing Strategy and Approaches

sections.title: Global Marketing Strategy and Glocalisation
sections.keyIdea: A global marketing strategy plans one marketing approach for the world market; glocalisation keeps that global core and adapts what local buyers need changed.

body.text: A **global marketing strategy** treats every country a firm sells in as one market. The brand, the core product and the message are planned once and used everywhere, as far as buyers allow.

The gain is scale. Serana, a Singaporean skincare brand sold in 6 countries, can make one advertising campaign for $1.2m and run it in all of them: $200,000 a country. Separate campaigns would cost $450,000 each, $2.7m in total. Standardising saves $1.5m, and buyers see the same brand wherever they travel.

The risk is that buyers are not the same everywhere. A message, a pack or a product that works at home can fail where beliefs, tastes or languages differ, and then the saving is paid for in lost sales.

**Global localisation**, or **glocalisation**, is the answer most global brands reach: "think global, act local". The firm keeps what gives it scale and recognition, such as the name, the logo and the core formula, and changes only the parts a country's buyers would otherwise reject.

realExample.text: An instant-noodle brand keeps its name, logo and cup design in every country, but sells a chicken version with no pork where many buyers avoid pork, and a hotter one where buyers prefer strong chilli.

sections.misconception: Students write that a global marketing strategy simply means selling in many countries. Selling in many countries is exporting; a global strategy is ONE plan for all of them. A firm in forty countries running forty unrelated campaigns does not have one.
sections.examMatters: When a case gives the cost of one campaign against several, work out the saving from standardising, then say what could be lost if buyers in one country reject the standard message.

recall.prompt: Put the steps in the order a firm follows to glocalise a product for a new market, from first to last.
recall.criterion: the order of the glocalisation decision, from first to last
correctOrder: Research the new market's culture, tastes and rules
Decide which parts of the mix stay global and which change
Test the adapted product and message with local buyers
Launch with the global brand and the local changes
why: Nothing can be adapted sensibly until the firm knows what differs in this market.
The research tells it what must change; everything else stays standard to keep the saving.
A trial with local buyers catches a wrong adaptation while it is still cheap to fix.
Only a tested mix is launched, carrying the global brand with its local changes.

sections.title: Ethnocentric and Polycentric Approaches
sections.keyIdea: An ethnocentric approach markets abroad the way it markets at home; a polycentric approach builds a separate marketing mix for each country.

body.text: A firm selling abroad can take one of three **marketing approaches**, and each answers the same question: whose view of the customer shapes the marketing?

A **domestic** or **ethnocentric** approach starts from home. The firm sells abroad the product, pack, price structure and adverts it designed for home buyers, assuming that what sells at home will sell elsewhere. It is cheap and quick, because nothing is redesigned, and head office keeps control. It works when the product meets the same need everywhere; it fails when buyers abroad differ from buyers at home.

An **international** or **polycentric** approach starts from each country. Every market is treated as different, usually with a local team deciding the mix there, so the product, the price, the channels and the message can all differ. It gives the closest fit to local buyers, but it costs more, gives up the saving from one campaign, and can leave the brand looking different in every country.
The two sit at opposite ends: one mix for everyone, designed at home, against a new mix for each country, designed there.

realExample.text: A juice maker in Kenya first sold its home packs and adverts unchanged in two neighbouring countries. When it entered a market with a different language and diet, it handed pack design and flavours to a team based there.

sections.misconception: Students confuse an ethnocentric approach with a global marketing strategy, because both use one mix. The difference is where the mix comes from: ethnocentric uses the HOME mix unchanged, while a global strategy is designed for the world market from the start.
sections.examMatters: Use the paired names the first time — "domestic/ethnocentric", "international/polycentric" — then explain the approach in terms of who decides the mix and how much of it changes.

recall.prompt: Sort each decision by the approach it shows: ethnocentric or polycentric.

groups.name: Ethnocentric
items: TV adverts made for viewers at home are aired abroad as they are
Head office issues one price list for every country
The home pack is exported with only the address changed
groups.why: The home market's mix is used abroad as it is, and the decision is taken at home.

groups.name: Polycentric
items: A team in each country picks its own flavours
Each country manager sets prices for that market
Every country gets its own brand name and adverts
groups.why: Each country's mix is designed for that country, usually by people working there.

sections.title: The Mixed/Geocentric Approach
sections.keyIdea: A geocentric approach sees the world as one market, keeps common what buyers share, and changes the rest; it is the approach behind glocalisation.

body.text: A **mixed** or **geocentric** approach takes neither home nor each separate country as its starting point. It looks at the world market as a whole, asks what buyers everywhere have in common, and standardises that; then it changes the elements where countries genuinely differ.

Serana works this way. One brand, one core formula and one global campaign serve all 6 countries, while each country team can choose pack sizes, a fragrance or the model in an advert. Decisions are shared between head office and the country teams rather than taken wholly by either.

Its strength is balance: most of the saving from standardising, with enough local fit to sell. Its weakness is that the line between shared and local has to be drawn and redrawn, which takes management time and causes disputes between head office and the countries.

Choosing between the three approaches turns on how alike the firm's buyers are, how costly a local mistake would be, and how much the firm can spend. A product that meets the same need everywhere leans towards one mix; one that touches food, faith or language leans towards local adaptation.

realExample.text: A phone-case brand designs one range and one online campaign for all its markets, but lets each country choose which colours to stock and translate the product pages.

sections.misconception: Students treat the mixed approach as automatically right because it sounds balanced. It has its own cost, the management time spent deciding what is shared, and a firm whose buyers are alike everywhere gains little from it.
sections.examMatters: A judgement between the approaches should name the condition that decides it, such as how alike buyers are or what a local mistake would cost, rather than choose the mixed approach as a safe middle.

recall.prompt: Name the approach each firm is taking:
template: A tea brand ships its home-market tins and posters abroad with no changes: the ___ approach.
A bank lets the team in every country design its own accounts, fees and adverts: the ___ approach.
A trainer brand shares its logo and designs worldwide, while sizes and adverts vary by country: the ___ approach.
hints: the home market is the reference point
every country is its own reference point
the world market as a whole is the reference point

takeaway: A global strategy is one plan for many countries; glocalisation adapts its edges.
Ethnocentric uses the home mix; polycentric designs one for each country.
Geocentric shares what buyers have in common and changes the rest.

content.title: The Marketing Mix in Global Markets

sections.title: Product: Standardise or Adapt?
sections.keyIdea: A product can travel unchanged or be adapted in its formula, size or label; the more it touches climate, law, belief or taste, the more it tends to change.

body.text: The **marketing mix (4Ps)** — product, price, place and promotion — has to be applied to every market a firm enters, and each P can be standardised or adapted. Product comes first, because the other three are built around it.

Some products travel unchanged: a phone charger meets the same need everywhere. Others need **adaptation** to the conditions of the market: its climate, its religious or legal rules on ingredients and labelling, its language, and how much and how often people buy.

Serana's core moisturiser is the same in every country. In Zarand, where the climate is hot and dry, it sells a lighter, alcohol-free gel, labelled in Zarand's own language. The brand, the logo and the core formula stay the same.
Every adaptation costs something: a separate production run, new packaging, more stock to hold. So a firm adapts only where the standard version would lose more sales than the change costs.

realExample.text: Chocolate makers selling into hot countries use recipes that soften at a higher temperature, so bars survive the journey from warehouse to shop.

sections.misconception: Students write that adapting the product always raises sales. It raises sales only where buyers would reject the standard version; elsewhere it adds cost for no gain, and too many versions weaken one recognisable brand.
sections.examMatters: Name the local condition that forces the change, such as climate, law, belief, income or taste, and the P it changes. An adaptation with no reason attached is description, not application.

recall.prompt: Match each product change to the local condition that calls for it.

pairs.left: A thinner lotion that dries in seconds
pairs.why: Heavy creams feel greasy and slide off in hot, damp weather.

pairs.left: Ingredients certified as permitted by a faith
pairs.right: Buyers whose religion restricts what they use
pairs.why: For these buyers an uncertified product is not an option at all.

pairs.left: A pack reprinted with new wording and warnings
pairs.why: The law and the reader both need the pack in the local language.

pairs.left: A pack a tenth of the usual size
pairs.right: Shoppers who buy a little at a time
pairs.why: Buyers with little cash to spare at once buy small amounts often.

sections.title: Price: Incomes, Pack Sizes and Local Rivals
sections.keyIdea: Price is adapted to what buyers can pay, what local rivals charge and what it costs to reach the market; changing the pack size is how many firms reach a price.

body.text: Price is the P most often changed, because incomes, local rivals and the cost of reaching a country all differ. One price in dollars can be a bargain in one market and a luxury in the next.

Where incomes are low, the obstacle is often the **price of one purchase**, not the price per ml. Serana's 200 ml bottle sells at $18, which is $0.09 a ml. A 25 ml **sachet** at $3 is $0.12 a ml, a third more, yet the buyer needs only a sixth of the money at the till.

That move changes two Ps, and good answers separate them. Making the smaller pack is a **product** decision, because the size of what is sold changes. Charging a price for it is a **price** decision, because it sets what one purchase costs.

Price is also set against local rivals — lower where cheap local brands are strong, higher where a foreign brand carries status — and it must cover the tariffs and freight that buyers at home never pay for.

realExample.text: Shampoo, coffee and detergent are widely sold in single-use packs in lower-income markets, so a household can buy a few days' supply with the cash it has that day.

sections.misconception: Students assume a small pack is cheaper for the buyer. It is cheaper per purchase but usually dearer per ml, so a buyer who relies on small packs pays more over a month than one who can afford the large size.
sections.examMatters: If a case gives pack sizes and prices, work out the price per unit of each: it shows whether the adaptation made the product cheaper or only easier to afford at once.

recall.prompt: Name the P each decision belongs to:
template: A coffee brand swaps its jar for a single-cup stick, changing how much is sold at once: a ___ decision.
It then asks a few cents for each stick, so one purchase fits a daily budget: a ___ decision.
hints: what the buyer receives has changed
what the buyer hands over has changed

sections.title: Place and Promotion Abroad
sections.keyIdea: Place follows how and where buyers in each country shop; promotion follows what they watch, read and believe, and what the law allows.

body.text: **Place** is adapted to how a country shops. In one market supermarkets dominate; in another most goods are bought from small family shops, open markets, or online and delivered. A firm that uses only the channels it knows at home can leave most buyers unreached.

Serana sells mainly through pharmacies at home. In Zarand most skincare is bought in small shops and online, so it appoints a local distributor for the small shops and sells direct through its own website.

**Promotion** is the P where culture matters most. The media people use differ, and so do what an advert may show, which public figures people trust, what humour works and what the law allows; some countries restrict adverts aimed at children or adverts that name a rival.
A global campaign can keep one message and one visual style while changing the language, the people and the setting in each country: the promotional form of glocalisation.

realExample.text: A sports-drink brand runs one global advert idea, an athlete pushing past exhaustion, but films each country's version with a well-known local athlete, in the local language.

sections.misconception: Students treat translating an advert as adapting it. A translation changes the words; adaptation may change the images, the setting, the people and the media used, because a message that is accurate can still be unwelcome.
sections.examMatters: Say which channel or medium the buyers in the case actually use, and why the home approach would not reach them. That turns a list of Ps into application.

recall.prompt: Sort each change into place or promotion.

groups.name: Place
items: Stocking corner kiosks instead of hypermarkets
Shipping web orders to remote villages
Appointing an agent who supplies rural stores
groups.why: These change where and how buyers get hold of the product.

groups.name: Promotion
items: Hiring a local film star for the campaign
Moving the budget from television to a messaging app
Dropping a slogan that mocks a rival brand
groups.why: These change how buyers hear about the product and what they are told.

takeaway: Each P can be standardised or adapted; adapt only where it pays.
A smaller pack is a product change that makes one purchase affordable.
Place follows how buyers shop; promotion follows what they accept.

content.title: Ansoff and Porter in Global Marketing

sections.title: Ansoff's Matrix Applied to Global Decisions
sections.keyIdea: Applied abroad, Ansoff's matrix sorts a firm's global options by whether the product and the market are new to it, and shows how risk rises as more is new.

body.text: **Ansoff's matrix** (a Unit 3 theory of corporate strategy, 3.3.1) asks two questions of any growth option: is the product one the firm already sells, and is the market one it already sells in? In global marketing the market is usually a country, or a group of buyers in one.
Serana's four options, one in each cell:

items: **Market penetration**: sell more of its existing moisturiser in the 6 countries it already serves, with more promotion.
**Market development**: take the existing moisturiser to Zarand, where it has never sold.
**Product development**: launch a new sun-protection range for buyers in its existing 6 countries.
**Diversification**: launch a hair-care range in Zarand, a new product in a new country.

body.text: Risk rises as more becomes new. Market development abroad adds the unknowns of a new country (culture, law, channels) to a product the firm knows works; diversification abroad adds both unknowns at once, which is why firms usually enter a country with a proven product first.

The test for the two middle cells is which element changed. Adapting an existing product so it sells in a new country, with a new label or pack size, is still **market development**, because the country is what is new. **Product development** is a genuinely new product for buyers the firm already has.

realExample.text: A frozen-food maker entering a new region usually starts with its best-selling existing meals, which is market development, and develops new dishes for buyers there only once it knows them.

sections.misconception: Students call any change made for a foreign market "product development". Relabelling or resizing an existing product for a new country is market development; product development means a new product for buyers the firm already serves.
sections.examMatters: Place the option in one cell, say which element is new, and use the cell to judge risk; then say what in the case makes that risk larger or smaller than the matrix suggests.

recall.prompt: Match each of a juice brand's moves to its cell in Ansoff's matrix.

pairs.left: Extra advertising for its orange juice at home
pairs.why: Same product, same market: it is selling more of what it already sells, where it already sells.

pairs.left: Its orange juice exported unchanged to a new country
pairs.why: The juice is proven; only the country is new.

pairs.left: A new vitamin drink for its home-country buyers
pairs.why: The buyers are existing ones; only the product is new.

pairs.left: A bottled-water range in a country it has never supplied
pairs.why: Both the product and the market are new, so both sets of unknowns arrive together.

sections.title: Porter's Matrix Applied to Global Decisions
sections.keyIdea: Porter's matrix asks how a firm will win abroad, on lower cost or on difference, and whether it targets the whole global market or one part of it.

body.text: **Porter's Strategic Matrix** (also 3.3.1) asks two things: does the firm's advantage come from lower cost or from offering something different, and does it aim at a broad market or a narrow one? Applied to global marketing, the answers shape the mix in every country.

**Cost leadership** across the world means one standard product made at great scale and sold on price; it fits a global marketing strategy, because every local version adds cost. **Differentiation** across the world means a product buyers value for something rivals lack, such as quality, design or a trusted brand, with one consistent image and a price that covers it.

**Cost focus** and **differentiation focus** aim at one part of the market. Globally, that part is often a group of buyers spread across many countries. Serana's halal-certified, alcohol-free serum is differentiation focus: something distinctive, built for one group, sold wherever that group lives.
The position limits the mix. A cost leader cannot afford many local versions; a differentiator can adapt more, but must keep what makes it distinctive the same everywhere.

realExample.text: A low-cost stationery maker sells the same pens in the same packs in dozens of countries and competes on price; a rival sells hand-bound notebooks at many times the price to collectors in the same countries.

sections.misconception: Students equate cost leadership with charging the lowest price. It means having the lowest cost; a global cost leader may price at the market level and earn a wider margin, cutting price only when it chooses to.
sections.examMatters: Place the firm in one cell with evidence from the case, then say what that position means for the 4Ps abroad, especially how much local adaptation it can afford.

recall.prompt: Sort each global position by where its advantage comes from: lower cost or difference.

groups.name: Lower cost
items: One standard charger made in vast volumes and sold on price in fifty countries
The cheapest supplier of uniforms to international schools
An airline flying one aircraft type on every route to keep costs down
groups.why: Each wins by supplying more cheaply than rivals, broadly or to one group.

groups.name: Difference
items: A luxury watch with the same prestige image in every country
Gluten-free baking mixes for coeliac buyers worldwide
Hand-finished guitars for professional players across the world
groups.why: Each wins because buyers value something rivals do not offer, broadly or to one group.

sections.title: Using Both Matrices for a Global Decision
sections.keyIdea: Ansoff's matrix says where a firm grows and how risky that is; Porter's says how it will compete once there. A global marketing decision needs both answers.

body.text: The two matrices answer different questions, so a global marketing decision usually needs both. Ansoff asks **where**: which products, in which countries, at what risk. Porter asks **how**: on what basis the firm will beat rivals once it is there.

Serana entering Zarand with its existing moisturiser is market development. How it competes there is a separate choice. Against cheap local creams it cannot win on cost when it ships from Singapore, so it competes on difference, with halal certification, a gel texture and a trusted brand, and prices above local rivals.

The two answers together then shape the mix: a standard brand and core formula, an adapted pack and label, selected shops rather than every market stall, and promotion that stresses what makes the product different.

Neither matrix makes the decision. Ansoff says nothing about how large a market is or how well the firm understands it, and Porter's cells blur when a firm is low-cost in one country and premium in another. They organise the argument; the evidence in the case decides it.

realExample.text: A Nigerian fashion label taking its existing designs to buyers of Nigerian origin in several other countries is developing new markets, and it competes on its designs and fabrics rather than on price.

sections.misconception: Students use Ansoff's matrix to say how a firm should compete, or Porter's to say which country it should enter. Each answers only its own question, so using one for the other's job misapplies both.
sections.examMatters: In a longer answer, use Ansoff to judge the risk of the move and Porter to judge whether the firm can win once there; the conclusion weighs the two.

recall.prompt: Sort each question by the matrix that answers it: Ansoff's or Porter's.

groups.name: Ansoff's matrix
items: Should we sell our existing range in a new country?
Is a new product in a new country too risky for us?
Should we push for more sales where we already sell?
groups.why: These are about which products in which markets, and the risk of the move.

groups.name: Porter's matrix
items: Should we compete on the lowest cost or on being different?
Should we target every buyer or one group of them?
Can our quality justify charging more than local rivals?
groups.why: These are about the basis of competition and how wide the target is.

takeaway: Ansoff: which is new, the product or the country, and how risky is it?
Porter: win abroad on lower cost or on difference, broadly or in a niche.
Use Ansoff for where and Porter for how; the evidence decides.

content.title: Global Niche Markets

sections.title: Cultural Diversity: Different Interests and Values
sections.keyIdea: Cultural diversity means groups of people across the globe have different interests and values, and a group that shares them can be a market wherever it lives.

body.text: **Cultural diversity** is the recognition that groups of people across the globe have different interests and values. A country is not one market of identical buyers: within it are groups with their own beliefs, customs and ways of spending their time.

Two kinds of difference matter for marketing. **Values** are beliefs about what is right or important: a faith's rules, a commitment to protecting animals, a view of how people should dress. **Interests** are what people enjoy or spend time on: a sport, a kind of music, a hobby.

Shared values and interests are what create global niches. A group that shares a value or an interest is often **spread across many countries**. It may be a small share of any one country and still, added together, a large number of people with the same need.

So cultural diversity works in two directions. It is a reason to adapt the mix country by country, and it is also a reason to look for groups that cross borders and serve them in the same way everywhere.

realExample.text: Fans of Korean pop music are a small part of the population in most countries, yet together they support merchandise, streaming and concert businesses worldwide.

sections.misconception: Students assume everyone in a country shares one culture, so a market can be described by its nationality. Within one country are groups with different values and interests, and some have more in common with people abroad than with their neighbours.
sections.examMatters: Name the value or interest the group in the case shares, and whether it crosses borders: that tells you whether to adapt by country or to serve one group in many countries.

recall.prompt: Sort each group by what binds it together: a shared value or a shared interest.

groups.name: A shared value
items: Vegans who refuse anything made from animals
Families who eat only food prepared under religious law
Buyers who pay more for goods made without child labour
groups.why: What unites each group is a belief about what is right or proper.

groups.name: A shared interest
items: Members of amateur astronomy clubs
Collectors of vintage wristwatches
People who run marathons for fun
groups.why: What unites each group is something its members enjoy doing.

sections.title: Features of Global Niche Markets
sections.keyIdea: A global niche is a small, specialised group of buyers with a shared need, spread across countries: small in each, worth serving in total, and often willing to pay more.

body.text: A **niche market** is a small, clearly defined part of a larger market, with needs the mass market serves badly. A **global niche** is that kind of group spread across many countries.
Its features:

items: **Small in each country, large in total.** Serana's halal-certified, alcohol-free serum has 60,000 likely buyers in one country and 15,000 in another; across five countries, 160,000.
**A specialised need shared across borders**, so one product can serve the whole group with little change.
**Less direct competition**, because firms serving the mass market find the group too small to target in any one country.
**Higher prices and margins**: buyers who cannot easily find the product elsewhere pay more. Serana charges $30 against $20 for a mass-market serum.
**Buyers who find each other** through communities, websites and specialist shops built around the need.

body.text: The weaknesses come from the same features. Sales are capped by the size of the group, one new rival can take a large share of it, and a firm that depends on one niche has no other market to fall back on.

realExample.text: A maker of left-handed guitars sells only a few hundred instruments in any one country, but by selling online it serves left-handed players everywhere with a single range.

sections.misconception: Students define a niche market as simply a small market. What defines it is a specialised need shared by a distinct group; a small town is a small market, not a niche.
sections.examMatters: Use the case's figures to show the niche is small in each country but viable in total, then weigh the higher price against the risk of depending on one group.

recall.prompt: Match each feature of a global niche to what it means for the firm serving it.

pairs.left: Buyers are few in any one country
pairs.right: It must sell in many countries to reach enough of them
pairs.why: Only the total across borders makes the group worth serving.

pairs.left: Few other firms meet the need
pairs.right: It can charge more than a mass-market product
pairs.why: Buyers with few alternatives accept a higher price.

pairs.left: The need is the same across borders
pairs.right: One version can be sold almost everywhere
pairs.why: Little adaptation is needed when the group wants the same thing wherever it lives.

pairs.left: The group gathers in its own communities
pairs.right: It can reach buyers without mass advertising
pairs.why: Promotion can go straight to where the group already meets.

sections.title: Adapting the 4Ps to Suit a Global Niche
sections.keyIdea: For a global niche the product usually stays the same everywhere, while price, place and promotion are set by the niche rather than by the country.

body.text: The **marketing mix (4Ps)** for a global niche is built around the group, not the country, so its adaptation follows the group. The usual question, what changes in each country, turns into another: what does this group need wherever it lives?

**Product.** The specialised feature is why the niche buys, so it stays the same everywhere: Serana's serum is halal-certified and alcohol-free in all five countries. Changes are limited to what law requires, such as the label.

**Price.** Buyers with few alternatives accept a higher price: $30 against $20, 50% more. It must still fit what the group can pay, so a firm may hold one price in richer markets and a lower one where incomes are lower.
**Place.** A niche is too thin to fill every supermarket shelf, so it is reached through shops that serve that need, outlets run by the community itself, and online orders shipped across borders.
**Promotion.** Rather than mass advertising, the firm goes where the group already gathers: its magazines and websites, community events, and recommendations from trusted members.

realExample.text: A small brand of vegan hiking boots sells from one website to walkers in dozens of countries, advertises in outdoor and vegan communities, and is never stocked by a mainstream shoe shop.

sections.misconception: Students adapt a niche product country by country, as they would a mass-market one. Changing the feature the niche buys for removes the reason it buys; for a global niche the product is the P that should stay the same.
sections.examMatters: For each P, say how serving the niche changes it compared with a mass-market mix, and use the case's figures for the price where they are given.

recall.prompt: Complete the mix of a gluten-free bakery brand selling to coeliac buyers in ten countries:
template: It sells at a ___ price well above ordinary bread, which its buyers accept.
It is stocked in health-food and other ___ shops, not in every supermarket.
hints: shops that serve one particular need

takeaway: Groups share values or interests across borders.
A global niche is small in each country and viable in total.
Keep the niche product the same; set price, place and promotion by the group.

content.title: Cultural and Social Factors

sections.title: Cultural Differences and Different Tastes
sections.keyIdea: Cultural differences decide what is acceptable to sell and show; different tastes and preferences decide what buyers like. Either can force a change to the mix.

body.text: Before selling in a new country, a business has four cultural and social factors to consider: cultural differences, different tastes and preferences, language and unintended meanings, and inappropriate branding and promotion. This step takes the first two.

**Cultural differences** are differences in beliefs, customs, religion and social rules: what may be eaten or worn, which days are holidays or fasts, who in a family makes buying decisions, what is polite or offensive to show. They decide whether a product, an ingredient or an image is acceptable at all.

**Different tastes and preferences** are differences in what buyers like: flavours, textures, sizes, colours and styles. They decide whether an acceptable product is wanted. Buyers in Zarand prefer light skincare in the heat; buyers in cooler countries may prefer rich creams.

A cultural difference can make a product unsaleable, so it is usually a condition to meet. A difference in taste usually lowers sales rather than stopping them, so it is a choice to weigh against the cost of adapting.

realExample.text: Snack makers selling across Asia commonly keep one brand but sell different flavours in each market, such as seaweed in one and chilli in another, while checking that no flavour uses an ingredient local faiths forbid.

sections.misconception: Students treat every cultural factor as a taste that a firm may ignore if adapting is expensive. A belief about what may be eaten or shown is not a preference, and ignoring it can make the product unsaleable.
sections.examMatters: Separate the two: a cultural difference that forbids something is a condition to meet; a taste is a trade-off between the cost of adapting and the sales it wins.

recall.prompt: Sort each consideration into a cultural difference or a difference in tastes and preferences.

groups.name: Cultural difference
items: Many buyers may not use products that contain alcohol
Adverts may not show couples embracing in public
Gifts are bought for a festival the home market does not hold
groups.why: Each comes from a belief, custom or rule about what is acceptable.

groups.name: Tastes and preferences
items: Buyers like sweeter biscuits than at home
Family-size packs outsell single ones
Spicy flavours outsell mild ones
groups.why: Each comes from what buyers like, not from what they are allowed.

sections.title: Language and Unintended Meanings
sections.keyIdea: A name, slogan or instruction can carry a meaning nobody intended once it is translated, or even when it is left untranslated and heard in a new language.

body.text: Language is the most visible way a global brand can go wrong, and **unintended meanings** arise in three places:

items: **The brand name.** It is usually left untranslated, so its sound is heard in every language, and it can sound like a rude, silly or unlucky word.
**The slogan or advert.** Idioms, puns and jokes rarely survive translation word for word, and can come out meaning something odd or offensive.
**The pack and instructions.** A mistranslated dose or warning is a safety and legal problem, not only an embarrassment.

body.text: Serana found that its name, spoken in Zarand's main language, sounds close to the word for "slippery". Before launching it asked people who grew up speaking that language what they heard, found most read the name as intended when it appeared beside the logo, and chose a local tagline that made the meaning clear.

The checks cost little next to a failed launch: ask local speakers what a name or slogan suggests to them, carry the idea across rather than the literal words, and have a second translator turn the text back into the original to see whether it still says what was meant.

realExample.text: A furniture brand preparing an export catalogue found that three of its product names, chosen in its home language, were slang words in the new market, and renamed them before printing.

sections.misconception: Students think unintended meanings arise only when a name is translated. An untranslated name is heard in the local language too, so a brand that never changes its name still has to check what it sounds like.
sections.examMatters: Explain the consequence, not only the error: ridicule that spreads, lost trust, the cost of renaming and reprinting, or a safety risk from a mistranslated instruction.

recall.prompt: Match each language problem to the check that would have caught it.

pairs.right: Trying the name out on local speakers before launch
pairs.why: Only people who use the language every day hear what the sound suggests.

pairs.left: A pun in the slogan that means nothing once translated
pairs.right: Rewriting the message around its idea for local buyers
pairs.why: Wordplay depends on one language, so the idea has to be re-expressed, not the words.

pairs.left: A dosage line that no longer matches the original

sections.title: Inappropriate Branding and Promotion
sections.keyIdea: Branding and promotion become inappropriate when a colour, symbol, image or message offends local beliefs, breaks local rules, or means something unintended there.

body.text: **Branding** is the name, logo, colours, symbols and pack design that identify a product. **Promotion** is how it is communicated: adverts, sponsorship, social media posts and offers. Either can be **inappropriate** in a new market, even after succeeding at home.

Branding goes wrong through meaning. Colours carry different associations in different cultures, so a colour linked with celebration in one place can be linked with mourning in another; animals, hand gestures, numbers and religious symbols can also carry meanings the firm never intended.

Promotion goes wrong through content and timing. An advert showing behaviour that is normal at home, such as how people dress or what they drink, can offend; humour can insult; a campaign timed carelessly around a religious or national occasion looks disrespectful. Some countries also ban certain kinds of advert.

steps.title: An inappropriate pack or advert
steps.subtitle: it offends, or means something unintended

steps.title: Buyers feel disrespected
steps.subtitle: they stop buying and tell others

steps.title: The mistake spreads online
steps.subtitle: it is seen in every market, not only one

body.result: The cost is lost sales, a weaker brand everywhere, and the cost of replacing packs and campaigns.

body.text: Serana has every pack and advert checked by its team in the country before it runs.

realExample.text: A gift-wrap exporter found that one of its best-selling colours was associated with funerals in one of its markets, and withdrew that colour from the range for that country only.

sections.misconception: Students treat inappropriate promotion as a translation problem only. Most promotional mistakes are in the images, the behaviour shown, the humour or the timing, and would offend even if every word were translated correctly.
sections.examMatters: Say what made the branding or promotion inappropriate in that market, the likely effect on sales and reputation, and the check the firm could have made before launch.

recall.prompt: Sort each mistake into inappropriate branding or inappropriate promotion.

items: A television joke that mocks a local custom
A discount offer run on a day of national grief

takeaway: A cultural difference is a condition; a taste is a trade-off.
Check what a name or slogan sounds like to local speakers.
Images, colours and timing can offend even when the words are right.

notes.title: Global Marketing Strategy and Approaches
notes.keyIdea: One plan for the world, adapted at the edges; and three approaches that differ in whose view of the buyer shapes the mix.

items.text: Global marketing strategy — one marketing approach planned for every country the firm sells in, standardised as far as buyers allow.
Glocalisation (global localisation) — "think global, act local": a global core with local adaptations.
Domestic/ethnocentric — the home mix sold abroad unchanged. International/polycentric — a separate mix for each country. Mixed/geocentric — shared where buyers are alike, adapted where they differ.
Scale: one campaign $1.2m for 6 countries against 6 × $450,000 = $2.7m; saving $1.5m.
The more a product touches faith, food or language, the further it moves from one standard mix.

takeaway: One plan, adapted at the edges.
Home mix, country mix, or shared core.
Name what decides it.

notes.title: The Marketing Mix in Global Markets
notes.keyIdea: Each of the 4Ps can be standardised or adapted to a global market, and each adaptation has a cost.

items.text: Product adaptation — changing formula, size, ingredients or label for local climate, law, belief, language or buying habits.
Price adaptation — setting price to local incomes, rivals and the cost of reaching the market.
Place and promotion — the channels buyers use, and the media, images and messages they accept.
Pack size: 200 ml at $18 ($0.09 a ml) against 25 ml at $3 ($0.12 a ml). The size is product; what one purchase costs is price.
Adapt only where the standard version would lose more sales than the change costs.

takeaway: Standardise or adapt, P by P.
Size is product; one purchase is price.
Tie each change to a local condition.

notes.title: Ansoff and Porter in Global Marketing
notes.keyIdea: Ansoff's matrix and Porter's matrix, both met in Unit 3 (3.3.1), applied to where a firm grows abroad and how it competes there.

items.text: Ansoff abroad — market penetration, market development (existing product, new country), product development (new product, existing buyers), diversification (both new).
Porter abroad — cost leadership or differentiation across the world market; cost focus or differentiation focus for one group, often a global niche.
Risk rises as more is new: diversification abroad adds an unknown product to an unknown country.
A cost leader cannot afford many local versions; a differentiator keeps its distinctive feature the same everywhere.
Adapting an existing product for a new country is still market development.

takeaway: Ansoff: where, and how risky.
Porter: how to win.
Both, then the evidence.

notes.title: Global Niche Markets
notes.keyIdea: Groups with shared values or interests cross borders; a global niche serves one such group everywhere with a mix built around it.

items.text: Cultural diversity — recognition that groups of people across the globe have different interests and values.
Global niche market — a small, specialised group with a shared need, spread across many countries.
Price: $30 against $20 for a mass-market serum, a 50% premium.
Keep the feature the niche buys for; set price, place and promotion by the group.

takeaway: Values and interests cross borders.
Small in each, viable in total.
The product stays; the rest follows the group.

notes.title: Cultural and Social Factors
notes.keyIdea: Four considerations before selling abroad: cultural differences, different tastes and preferences, language and unintended meanings, and inappropriate branding and promotion.

items.text: Cultural differences — beliefs, customs, religion and social rules that decide what is acceptable.
Tastes and preferences — what buyers like: flavours, textures, sizes, colours, styles.
Unintended meaning — a name, slogan or instruction that says something unplanned in another language.
Checks: local speakers hear the name first; translate the idea, not the words; translate back to test.
An offensive pack or advert → buyers feel disrespected → the mistake spreads online to every market.

takeaway: Condition or trade-off?
Test names with local speakers.
Images and timing offend too.

quiz.question: A firm keeps its brand name and logo the same in every country, but sells a different flavour where local buyers prefer it. This is:
quiz.explanation: A global core (name and logo) with a local change (the flavour) is glocalisation: think global, act local. An ethnocentric approach would change nothing, diversification is a new product in a new market, and cost leadership is a way of competing, not a way of adapting.

quiz.question: A firm sells abroad exactly the pack, price list and adverts it designed for buyers at home. Its marketing approach is:
quiz.explanation: Using the home mix unchanged abroad is the domestic, or ethnocentric, approach. A polycentric approach would design a separate mix for each country, a geocentric one would share some elements and adapt others, and differentiation focus is a position in Porter's matrix.

quiz.question: The main advantage of a global marketing strategy over separate plans for each country is:
options: a closer fit to each country's tastes
the saving from planning once for many countries
local teams choosing their own mix
no risk of offending any buyers
quiz.explanation: Planning one brand, product and campaign for every country spreads the cost of making them, which is the scale a global strategy is for. A closer local fit and local teams are the strengths of a polycentric approach, and a standard message raises the risk of offending somebody rather than removing it.

quiz.question: One advertising campaign for eight countries costs $1.6m. A separate campaign for each country would cost $300,000 per country. Using the one campaign saves:
quiz.explanation: Eight separate campaigns cost 8 × $300,000 = $2.4m, and the single campaign costs $1.6m, so standardising saves $0.8m. Subtracting one country's campaign from the global one, or quoting either total on its own, misses the comparison.

quiz.question: Which approach gives the managers in each country the power to design their own marketing mix?
quiz.explanation: A polycentric approach treats every country as its own market, usually with a local team deciding the mix there. An ethnocentric approach decides at home, a geocentric one shares decisions between head office and the countries, and a global strategy plans one mix for all.

quiz.question: A geocentric approach differs from an ethnocentric one because it:
options: plans for the world market, not from the home market
lets every country design its own mix
sells only in the home market
quiz.explanation: Both can use one core mix, but the geocentric approach builds it from what buyers everywhere share and adapts the rest, while the ethnocentric approach exports the home mix as it is. Letting every country design its own mix is polycentric.

quiz.question: A firm's standard advert shows friends drinking beer at a family meal. In a market where most buyers do not drink alcohol, the main risk of an ethnocentric approach is that the advert:
options: costs more to make than a local one
loses the firm its economies of scale
offends the buyers it is meant to win
lets local managers change the brand
quiz.explanation: An ethnocentric approach runs the home advert unchanged, so behaviour that is normal at home is shown to buyers who may find it offensive. Running the same advert is cheaper, not dearer, keeps the scale saving, and leaves decisions at head office.

quiz.question: A detergent brand sells a 1 kg box for $4.00 and a 50 g sachet for $0.25. Per gram, the sachet is:
quiz.explanation: The box costs $4.00 ÷ 1,000 g = $0.004 a gram and the sachet $0.25 ÷ 50 g = $0.005 a gram, which is 25% more. The sachet is cheaper per purchase, not per gram; 20% is the gap measured against the sachet's price instead of the box's.

quiz.question: A shampoo brand starts selling single-use sachets alongside its full bottles, so buyers on low incomes can afford one purchase. Which two Ps has it changed?
quiz.explanation: The sachet is a different size of what is sold, which is a product decision, and it lets one purchase cost little, which is a price decision. Nothing in the stem changes where the shampoo is sold or how it is advertised.

quiz.question: In a country where most goods are bought from small family-run shops, a firm used to selling through supermarkets will most need to adapt its:
quiz.explanation: Place is how the product reaches buyers, and here the channel the firm knows reaches few of them, so it needs distributors or agents who supply small shops. The other Ps may also change, but the channel is the one the situation forces.

quiz.question: A global campaign keeps one message but is filmed in each country with local actors speaking the local language. This adapts:
quiz.explanation: The message and brand stay global while the people and language change, which is glocalisation applied to promotion. Nothing about the product, the channel or the price has changed.

quiz.question: Why might a firm's price abroad be higher than its price at home?
options: buyers abroad earn more in every case
one global price is required by law
rivals abroad never cut their prices
tariffs and freight add to its cost there
quiz.explanation: Reaching a foreign market adds costs, such as tariffs and freight, that home buyers never pay, and the price has to cover them. Incomes abroad are not always higher, no rule fixes one global price, and local rivals often compete hard on price.

quiz.question: A firm competing abroad on having the lowest cost is least able to afford:
options: many local versions of its product
one standard product for every country
quiz.explanation: Every local version adds design, production and stock costs, which undermines the low cost the firm competes on. A standard product, long production runs and one global campaign are how a global cost leader keeps its cost down.

quiz.question: A drinks firm launches its existing cola, with a translated label, in a country where it has never sold. In Ansoff's matrix this is:
quiz.explanation: The cola is an existing product and the country is a new market, so the move is market development. A translated label does not make it a new product; product development would be a new drink for buyers the firm already has.

quiz.question: Compared with its other growth options in Ansoff's matrix, a new product sold in a new country is:
quiz.explanation: A new product in a new country is diversification, and it carries the unknowns of both at once, so it is the riskiest cell. Market penetration, with nothing new, is the least risky, and the two middle cells each change only one element.

quiz.question: A brand sells a distinctive product to one group of buyers spread across many countries. In Porter's Strategic Matrix its position is:
quiz.explanation: Its advantage is being different, and its target is one group rather than the whole market, which is differentiation focus. Differentiation aims at the whole market, and the cost positions win on lower cost.

quiz.question: Which question does Porter's matrix answer that Ansoff's matrix does not?
options: which country the firm should enter
on what basis the firm will beat rivals
whether the product is new to the firm
how risky entering a new market is
quiz.explanation: Porter's matrix is about how a firm competes: lower cost or difference, broad or narrow. Which market to enter, whether the product is new and how risky the move is are the questions Ansoff's matrix sorts.

quiz.question: A brand sells prayer mats to Muslim buyers in thirty countries. The group it serves is defined mainly by a shared:
quiz.explanation: The buyers are united by their faith, a belief about what is right, which is a shared value. They live in thirty countries, so nationality does not define them, and neither income nor climate is what they have in common.

quiz.question: Which of these is a feature of a global niche market?
options: buyers few in each country but many in total
low prices set against many rivals
a product changed for every country
quiz.explanation: A global niche is a specialised group spread thinly across countries, so it is worth serving only in total. Mass appeal is the opposite of a niche, niches usually face few direct rivals and pay a higher price, and the specialised product is kept the same.

quiz.question: A niche brand keeps the same specialised product in every country. The main reason is that:
options: the specialised feature is why the niche buys
adapting any product is against the law
every country has the same tastes
the firm wants to be the cost leader
quiz.explanation: The niche exists because of one specialised need, so changing that feature removes the reason to buy. Tastes do differ between countries, which is why a mass-market product is adapted, and a niche brand competes on focus, not on being the lowest-cost supplier to the whole market.

quiz.question: A niche serum sells for $36 when a mass-market serum sells for $30. The price premium is:
quiz.explanation: The premium is the extra $6 as a share of the mass-market price: 6 ÷ 30 = 20%. Dividing by the niche price gives about 17%, and $6 is the gap in dollars, not a percentage.

quiz.question: Before launch, which check would best catch a brand name that sounds like a rude word in the new market?
options: testing the price with local buyers
counting the shops that could stock it
asking local speakers what the name suggests
comparing the pack with local rivals
quiz.explanation: Only people who speak the language every day hear what the sound suggests, so asking them is the check that finds an unintended meaning. Price tests, shop counts and pack comparisons are useful, but none of them tests what the name means.

quiz.question: A shop runs a price promotion on a day when the country is mourning a national tragedy. This is an example of:
quiz.explanation: The offer is part of how the product is communicated, and its timing shows no respect for the occasion, so it is inappropriate promotion. Nothing about the name, logo or pack is wrong, and the problem is not what buyers like or what a word means.

quiz.question: Which of these is a difference in tastes and preferences rather than a cultural difference?
options: a rule against showing couples embracing
a festival the home market lacks
quiz.explanation: Liking sweeter biscuits is about what buyers enjoy, so it is a taste. A faith's rule, a rule about what may be shown and a festival are all beliefs or customs, which are cultural differences.

quiz.question: Why can a brand name that is never translated still carry an unintended meaning?
options: its sound is heard in the local language too
only translated names are checked by law
buyers abroad never see the logo
translation always changes a name's sound
quiz.explanation: Buyers hear an untranslated name in their own language, so it can sound like a rude or unlucky word there. Whether a name is translated has nothing to do with the law, buyers do see logos, and the sound of an untranslated name is not changed at all.

practice.question: Source A. Serana is a Singaporean skincare brand sold in 6 countries. It runs one advertising campaign in all of them, which cost $1.2m; a separate campaign for each country would cost about $450,000. Its directors now plan to enter Zarand, a hot, dry country where most people are Muslim and speak their own language. In Zarand most skincare is bought in small family shops and online, and cheap local creams are popular. Spoken in Zarand's language, the name Serana sounds close to the word for "slippery". Serana also makes a halal-certified, alcohol-free serum for Muslim buyers. It estimates the number of likely buyers in five countries at 40,000, 25,000, 60,000, 15,000, 20,000. Each buyer uses 3 bottles a year at $30 a bottle, against $20 for a mass-market serum. Its current options include taking its existing moisturiser to Zarand, and launching a new hair-care range there. Explain one way Ansoff's matrix could help Serana decide whether to enter Zarand. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Place the move in one cell of the matrix first, and check which element is new: the product, the country, or both. Then say what the cell tells the directors about the risk, compared with another option the source mentions.
Knowledge: Ansoff's matrix sorts growth options by whether the product and the market are existing or new, and risk rises as more is new (1 mark). Application: taking the existing moisturiser to Zarand is market development, because the country is new and the product is not; a new label or pack size would not make it a new product (1 mark). Analysis: so the risk lies in the unfamiliar country — small-shop channels, cheap local rivals, a name that sounds like "slippery" — rather than in a product that already sells (1 mark). Analysis: comparing it with launching hair care in Zarand, which is diversification with both elements new, shows the directors that the moisturiser is the lower-risk way in (1 mark). An answer that calls the adapted moisturiser "product development" has confused the cells and loses the application mark.

Serana also makes a halal-certified, alcohol-free serum for Muslim buyers. It estimates the number of likely buyers in five countries at 40,000, 25,000, 60,000, 15,000, 20,000. Each buyer uses 3 bottles a year at $30 a bottle, against $20 for a mass-market serum. Its current options include taking its existing moisturiser to Zarand, and launching a new hair-care range there. Calculate the annual revenue Serana would earn from its serum if every likely buyer in the five countries bought it. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Add up the buyers before anything else, then work out how many bottles they buy in a year, and only then turn bottles into revenue. Show each step on its own line and give the answer in dollars.
Total buyers: 40,000 + 25,000 + 60,000 + 15,000 + 20,000 = 160,000 (1 mark). Bottles a year: 160,000 × 3 = 480,000 (1 mark). Revenue: 480,000 × $30 (1 mark) = $14.4m a year (1 mark). An answer that uses the mass-market price of $20, or forgets that each buyer buys 3 bottles, has used the wrong figure for one step and keeps the marks for the others.

In Zarand most skincare is bought in small family shops and online, and cheap local creams are popular. Spoken in Zarand's language, the name Serana sounds close to the word for "slippery". Serana also makes a halal-certified, alcohol-free serum for Muslim buyers. It estimates the number of likely buyers in five countries at 40,000, 25,000, 60,000, 15,000, 20,000. Each buyer uses 3 bottles a year at $30 a bottle, against $20 for a mass-market serum. Its current options include taking its existing moisturiser to Zarand, and launching a new hair-care range there. Discuss the cultural and social factors Serana should consider before launching in Zarand. (8 marks)
practice.guidance:
Work through the factors the source gives evidence for rather than listing every one you know, and for each say what could go wrong for this brand. Leave room for a brief assessment of which factor matters most and why.
Level 1: names cultural or social factors with little use of the source. Level 2: knowledge and application — most buyers in Zarand are Muslim, so ingredients must be permitted (a cultural difference); the hot, dry climate suggests lighter textures (a difference in taste); the brand name sounds like "slippery" in the local language (an unintended meaning). Level 3: analysis of the consequences — an ingredient buyers may not use makes the product unsaleable, while a heavy texture only lowers sales; the name could invite ridicule that spreads online, and packs or adverts showing behaviour that is normal at home could offend. Level 4: a brief assessment of competing factors, for example that the cultural difference is a condition to meet while the name is a risk to test with local speakers, and that Serana's halal serum shows it already understands the first. Discuss needs this assessment; it does not need a final recommendation.

practice.question: Source A. Serana is a Singaporean skincare brand sold in 6 countries. It runs one advertising campaign in all of them, which cost $1.2m; a separate campaign for each country would cost about $450,000. Its directors now plan to enter Zarand, a hot, dry country where most people are Muslim and speak their own language. In Zarand most skincare is bought in small family shops and online, and cheap local creams are popular. Spoken in Zarand's language, the name Serana sounds close to the word for "slippery". Serana also makes a halal-certified, alcohol-free serum for Muslim buyers. It estimates the number of likely buyers in five countries at 40,000, 25,000, 60,000, 15,000, 20,000. Each buyer uses 3 bottles a year at $30 a bottle, against $20 for a mass-market serum. Its current options include taking its existing moisturiser to Zarand, and launching a new hair-care range there. Assess whether Serana should adapt its marketing mix for Zarand or keep its standard global mix. (12 marks)
practice.guidance:
Take the 4Ps one at a time and ask, for each, whether the standard version would lose sales in this market. Weigh what adapting would win against what it would cost, and decide before you write what your judgement will turn on.
Level 1: knowledge of standardisation and adaptation, described generally. Level 2: application to Zarand — small family shops and online buying mean the pharmacy channel used at home will not reach buyers (place); cheap local creams mean the standard price may look high (price); a hot, dry climate and Muslim buyers point to an alcohol-free, lighter formula (product). Level 3: analysis of both sides — adapting place and product wins buyers the standard mix would miss; against that, one campaign across 6 countries cost $1.2m where separate ones would cost about $450,000 each, so every adaptation erodes the saving and the consistent brand. Level 4: evaluation reaching a supported judgement, for example that Serana should keep its brand and core campaign but adapt place and product, because those are where the standard mix would fail outright, while price can compete on difference rather than match local creams.
A strong answer, in outline: keeping everything standard would fail on channel and formula; adapting everything would lose the saving and the brand; so a glocal mix is justified — the same brand and campaign, adapted place and product — and the judgement depends on how far local buyers value the brand over the cheaper local creams.

It runs one advertising campaign in all of them, which cost $1.2m; a separate campaign for each country would cost about $450,000. Its directors now plan to enter Zarand, a hot, dry country where most people are Muslim and speak their own language. In Zarand most skincare is bought in small family shops and online, and cheap local creams are popular. Spoken in Zarand's language, the name Serana sounds close to the word for "slippery". Serana also makes a halal-certified, alcohol-free serum for Muslim buyers. It estimates the number of likely buyers in five countries at 40,000, 25,000, 60,000, 15,000, 20,000. Each buyer uses 3 bottles a year at $30 a bottle, against $20 for a mass-market serum. Its current options include taking its existing moisturiser to Zarand, and launching a new hair-care range there. Assess whether Serana should compete in Zarand on low price or on being different. (12 marks)
practice.guidance:
Use Porter's Strategic Matrix to frame the choice, then look in the source for what decides it: who the rivals are, what they charge, and what this brand has that they do not. Your judgement should say which position is more likely to work and what it would depend on.
Level 1: knowledge of Porter's Strategic Matrix, described generally. Level 2: application — competing on low price would mean matching cheap local creams made without the cost of shipping from Singapore; competing on difference would rest on halal certification, an alcohol-free formula and an established brand. Level 3: analysis of both sides — a low-cost position needs scale and standard products that a newcomer in Zarand lacks, and would force many cost-cutting compromises; differentiation lets Serana price above local rivals if buyers value what is different, but only if the difference is visible and trusted, which the awkward name could undermine. Level 4: evaluation with a supported judgement, for example that differentiation is more realistic because Serana cannot be the lowest-cost supplier from abroad, provided the brand is presented so that buyers see its difference rather than hear an unfortunate word.
A strong answer, in outline: low price means fighting local creams on their own ground without their cost advantage; difference uses what the brand already has; so differentiation is the better position, and it depends on local buyers valuing halal certification and quality enough to pay more.

practice.question: Source A. Serana is a Singaporean skincare brand sold in 6 countries. It runs one advertising campaign in all of them, which cost $1.2m; a separate campaign for each country would cost about $450,000. Its directors now plan to enter Zarand, a hot, dry country where most people are Muslim and speak their own language. In Zarand most skincare is bought in small family shops and online, and cheap local creams are popular. Spoken in Zarand's language, the name Serana sounds close to the word for "slippery". Serana also makes a halal-certified, alcohol-free serum for Muslim buyers. It estimates the number of likely buyers in five countries at 40,000, 25,000, 60,000, 15,000, 20,000. Each buyer uses 3 bottles a year at $30 a bottle, against $20 for a mass-market serum. Its current options include taking its existing moisturiser to Zarand, and launching a new hair-care range there. Evaluate whether a mixed/geocentric approach is the most suitable marketing approach for Serana. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
Set out what each of the three approaches would mean for this brand in practice, using the source, before judging any of them. Then weigh the saving from one plan against the cost of getting a country wrong, and finish with a recommendation that says what would change it.
Level 1: describes one or more approaches with little reference to the source. Level 2: knowledge and application — an ethnocentric approach would take the home mix to Zarand unchanged; a polycentric one would design a new mix there, losing the benefit of one campaign that cost $1.2m against about $450,000 a country; a geocentric approach would keep the brand, formula and campaign and adapt what must change. Level 3: analysis — Zarand differs on channel, climate, religion and language, so an unchanged home mix risks failing outright, while a fully separate mix gives up scale across 6 countries and a consistent brand; the geocentric approach keeps most of the saving but needs head office and country teams to agree on what is shared. Level 4: evaluation — weighs these against the evidence, considers what is not in the source (the size of Zarand, how alike its buyers are to existing ones), and reaches a perceptive recommendation with conditions.
A strong answer, in outline: ethnocentric is cheapest but ignores the differences the source lists; polycentric fits Zarand best but throws away the saving and the single brand; geocentric keeps the global core and changes place, product and the local tagline, so it is the most suitable, unless Zarand proves so different, or so large, that a separate plan would pay for itself.

Its directors now plan to enter Zarand, a hot, dry country where most people are Muslim and speak their own language. In Zarand most skincare is bought in small family shops and online, and cheap local creams are popular. Spoken in Zarand's language, the name Serana sounds close to the word for "slippery". Serana also makes a halal-certified, alcohol-free serum for Muslim buyers. It estimates the number of likely buyers in five countries at 40,000, 25,000, 60,000, 15,000, 20,000. Each buyer uses 3 bottles a year at $30 a bottle, against $20 for a mass-market serum. Its current options include taking its existing moisturiser to Zarand, and launching a new hair-care range there. Evaluate whether Serana should give priority to the global niche for its serum rather than to launching its moisturiser in Zarand. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
Compare the two options on the same basis: how many buyers each reaches, what it earns, what it costs to serve, and how risky it is. Use the figures in the source where you can, then bring in what the figures do not show, and finish with a recommendation and the condition that would change it.
Level 1: describes niche or mass markets in general terms. Level 2: knowledge and application — the serum's niche is small in each country but 160,000 buyers in total, worth about $14.4m a year at $30 a bottle, a 50% premium over mass-market serum; Zarand is a new country for an existing moisturiser. Level 3: analysis — the niche buys for a feature Serana already has, faces few direct rivals and can be reached through its own communities, but the revenue estimate assumes every likely buyer buys, and depending on one group leaves the firm exposed if a large rival enters; Zarand offers a broad market but brings cheap local rivals, new channels and the name problem. Level 4: evaluation — judges which offers the better balance of return and risk for this firm, notes that the two are not exclusive, and reaches a perceptive recommendation with conditions.
A strong answer, in outline: the niche uses what Serana already does well, at a premium price, with few rivals; Zarand is larger but riskier and needs more adaptation; so the niche should come first, unless the revenue estimate proves optimistic or a large rival enters it, in which case the broader market matters more.

flashcards.front: What is a global marketing strategy?
flashcards.back: One marketing approach planned for every country a firm sells in, with the brand, core product and message standardised as far as buyers allow.

flashcards.front: What is glocalisation?
flashcards.back: Global localisation, "think global, act local": a global core (name, logo, formula) with local changes where buyers would otherwise reject the product.

flashcards.front: What is the main gain from standardising the mix?
flashcards.back: Scale: one product, pack and campaign are designed once and used everywhere, which costs far less than separate versions, and the brand is consistent.

flashcards.front: What is the domestic/ethnocentric approach?
flashcards.back: Selling abroad the mix designed for home buyers, unchanged, on the assumption that what sells at home sells everywhere.

flashcards.front: What is the international/polycentric approach?
flashcards.back: Treating each country as a separate market, with a mix designed for that country, usually by a local team.

flashcards.front: What is the mixed/geocentric approach?
flashcards.back: Treating the world as one market: standardising what buyers share and adapting what differs, with decisions shared between head office and countries.

flashcards.front: Ethnocentric or global strategy: what is the difference?
flashcards.back: Both can use one mix, but ethnocentric uses the HOME mix unchanged; a global strategy is designed for the world market from the start.

flashcards.front: When does a product need adapting for a new market?
flashcards.back: When the local climate, law, religion, language, income or buying habits would make buyers reject the standard version.

flashcards.front: Is a smaller pack a product or a price decision?
flashcards.back: Both. The size of what is sold is product; what one purchase costs is price. A good answer separates them.

flashcards.front: Why can a single-use pack be dearer per unit?
flashcards.back: It costs less per purchase but more per ml or gram, so it is easier to afford at once but not cheaper.

flashcards.front: Why is place often adapted abroad?
flashcards.back: Countries shop differently — supermarkets, small shops, markets, online — so the home channel can miss most buyers.

flashcards.front: Why is promotion the P where culture matters most?
flashcards.back: Media, trusted faces, humour, what may be shown and what the law allows all differ between countries.

flashcards.front: Ansoff abroad: what is market development?
flashcards.back: An existing product in a new country. Adapting its label or size does not make it a new product.

flashcards.front: Ansoff abroad: what is product development?
flashcards.back: A new product for buyers the firm already serves.

flashcards.front: Why is diversification abroad the riskiest option?
flashcards.back: Both the product and the country are new, so the firm faces the unknowns of each at once.

flashcards.front: Porter abroad: what does global cost leadership need?
flashcards.back: One standard product made at great scale; every local version adds cost, so adaptation is kept to a minimum.

flashcards.front: Porter abroad: what is differentiation focus?
flashcards.back: A distinctive product for one group of buyers, often a group spread across many countries: a global niche.

flashcards.front: Which question does each matrix answer?
flashcards.back: Ansoff: where to grow and how risky it is. Porter: how to compete once there. A global decision needs both.

flashcards.front: What is cultural diversity?
flashcards.back: Recognition that groups of people across the globe have different interests and values.

flashcards.front: Values or interests: what is the difference?
flashcards.back: Values are beliefs about what is right or important; interests are what people enjoy or spend time on.

flashcards.front: What is a global niche market?
flashcards.back: A small, specialised group of buyers with a shared need, spread across many countries.

flashcards.front: What are the features of a global niche?
flashcards.back: Small in each country but viable in total; a specialised shared need; few direct rivals; higher prices; buyers who gather in communities.

flashcards.front: How are the 4Ps adapted for a global niche?
flashcards.back: The product stays the same everywhere; price carries a premium; place uses specialist and online channels; promotion goes where the group gathers.

flashcards.front: Name the four cultural and social considerations.
flashcards.back: Cultural differences; different tastes and preferences; language and unintended meanings; inappropriate branding and promotion.

flashcards.front: Cultural difference or taste: why does it matter which?
flashcards.back: A cultural difference that forbids something is a condition to meet; a taste is a trade-off between the cost of adapting and the sales it wins.

flashcards.front: How can a firm avoid unintended meanings?
flashcards.back: Ask local speakers what names and slogans suggest, translate the idea rather than the words, and have a second translator translate back.

flashcards.front: How can branding be inappropriate abroad?
flashcards.back: A colour, symbol, animal, number or gesture in the name, logo or pack can mean something offensive or unlucky there.

flashcards.front: How can promotion be inappropriate abroad?
flashcards.back: Through what an advert shows, its humour, or its timing around a religious or national occasion, even if every word is correct.

mistakes.title: Treating standardisation and adaptation as all or nothing
mistakes.mistake: Writing that a firm must either standardise its whole mix or adapt all of it.
mistakes.correction: Each of the 4Ps can be decided separately. Most global brands keep the name and core product and adapt a pack, a channel or an advert: glocalisation.
mistakes.examTip: Go through the Ps one by one and say which should stay standard and which should change, with a reason from the case for each.

mistakes.title: Mixing up the three approaches
mistakes.mistake: Describing a firm that exports its home adverts unchanged as "polycentric", or a firm with a separate mix in each country as "ethnocentric".
mistakes.correction: Ethnocentric uses the home mix; polycentric designs one for each country; geocentric shares what buyers have in common and adapts the rest.
mistakes.examTip: Use the paired names (domestic/ethnocentric, international/polycentric, mixed/geocentric) and say who decides the mix.

mistakes.title: Calling a smaller pack a price decision only
mistakes.mistake: Writing that selling single-use sachets is "a pricing strategy" and stopping there.
mistakes.correction: The pack size is a product change; what one purchase costs is price. The sachet changes both, which is why it works in low-income markets.
mistakes.examTip: Name both Ps and explain how the product change makes the price affordable per purchase.

mistakes.title: Calling an adapted product "product development"
mistakes.mistake: Labelling an existing product with a translated pack, sold in a new country, as product development in Ansoff's matrix.
mistakes.correction: The product is not new; the country is. That is market development. Product development is a new product for buyers the firm already has.
mistakes.examTip: Ask which element is new, the product or the market, before naming the cell.

mistakes.title: Defining a niche as just a small market
mistakes.mistake: Writing that a global niche is any small market, such as a small country.
mistakes.correction: A niche is defined by a specialised need shared by a distinct group. A global niche is that group spread across countries: small in each, viable in total.
mistakes.examTip: Name the shared need and show, with figures if given, that the total across countries makes it worth serving.

mistakes.title: Treating every cultural factor as a taste
mistakes.mistake: Arguing that a firm can ignore a local belief if adapting is too expensive.
mistakes.correction: A belief about what may be eaten, worn or shown is a cultural difference and a condition of selling at all; only a taste is a trade-off against cost.
mistakes.examTip: Say which kind of difference the case shows before deciding whether the firm must adapt or may choose to.

mistakes.title: Explaining a language mistake without its consequence
mistakes.mistake: Stating that a brand name has an unfortunate meaning, and moving on.
mistakes.correction: The damage is in the consequences: ridicule that spreads online, lost trust, the cost of renaming and reprinting, or a safety risk from a mistranslated instruction.
mistakes.examTip: Follow the mistake to its effect on sales or reputation, then name the check that would have caught it.

chains.title: Glocalising a product for a new market
steps: Research the new market's culture, tastes and rules.
Decide which parts of the mix stay global and which change.
Test the adapted product and message with local buyers.
Launch with the global brand and the local changes.
chains.result: The brand stays global; only what local buyers would reject is changed, and it is tested before it costs a launch.

chains.title: How an unchanged home advert can lose a market
steps: A firm takes an ethnocentric approach and runs its home advert abroad.
The advert shows behaviour that is normal at home but offensive there.
Buyers feel the brand does not respect them and share their reaction online.
Sales fall, and the firm pays for a new campaign it could have made first.
chains.result: The saving from one campaign is real, but it is lost if one market rejects the message.

chains.title: Why a global niche can be worth serving
steps: A group shares a specialised need, but is small in every country.
Mass-market firms find it too small to target country by country.
A firm serves the whole group across borders with one product.
Few rivals and a loyal group support a premium price.
chains.result: Cultural diversity creates the niche; selling across countries makes it large enough to serve.

evaluation.title: Standardise or adapt?
evaluation.content: Neither is right in general. Standardising saves money — Serana's one campaign cost $1.2m against about $2.7m for separate ones — and keeps one brand. Adapting wins buyers who would reject the standard version. Three things decide it. THE PRODUCT: the more it touches food, faith, climate or language, the more it must change. THE MARKET: how different its buyers, channels and rules are from those the firm knows. THE COST: whether the extra sales cover the extra versions. The strongest conclusion says which Ps should change and which should not, and why.

evaluation.title: A global niche or a mass market?
evaluation.content: A niche offers a premium price and few rivals — Serana's serum sells at $30 against $20 — but its size is capped by the group, and one large rival can take much of it. A mass market offers volume and scale, but more competition and lower prices. The deciding questions are whether the firm has a feature the niche values that others cannot copy, and whether the niche's total across countries is large enough to justify serving it. The two are not exclusive: many firms serve a niche with one product and the mass market with another.

evaluation.title: How much can the two matrices tell you?
evaluation.content: Ansoff's matrix shows how risky a global move is by what is new, and Porter's matrix shows how the firm could win once there. Neither measures the size of a market, the strength of local rivals or how well the firm understands a country's culture, and a firm can sit in different cells in different countries. Use them to organise the argument, then let the evidence in the case decide it.
